extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and performers learning tag/tag-line technique
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and evaluative criteria for writing and placing tags (additional punchlines after the original punchline) in stand-up jokes to increase laughs and ride the original setup. Covers definition, functions, timing, and an explicit rubric for judging tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a tag
rubrics_metrics.description: A tag is the third element of a joke — any laugh line after the original punch line. A tag is an additional short punchline immediately following a punchline (or another tag) that does not require a new setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags occur after the original punchline and can follow another tag; they must not introduce a new setup. (Also reflected in the joke structure: with tags: setup → punchline → tag → tag → tag …)

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortness / no new setup
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the tag short (no new setup required)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tag should be concise and self-contained relative to the existing setup — it should not demand a separate setup. Shortness helps it land quickly and lets it ride the energy of the original laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of the same premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it extend the same premise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good tag keeps working the original premise rather than introducing an unrelated idea. It should stay within the logical world already established by the setup and original punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lands its own laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it land its own laugh (not just repeat)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags should produce an additional laugh rather than merely restating the punchline or milking the same joke. If it only repeats the original punch, it is weak; aim for a distinct laugh trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement timing — ride the original laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it placed close enough in time to ride the original laugh?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place tags immediately after the punchline (or previous tag) so they capitalize on the laugh's momentum. Waiting too long risks losing the audience's attention and the connective thread to the setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation / taking the premise further
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it take the premise further (escalate)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags often work by pushing the premise deeper or more extreme — escalating the logic or consequence to generate more surprise and humor. Escalation is a common mechanism for strong tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer an alternate angle or source perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer an opinion or angle from another source/perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tag can change viewpoint (e.g., introduce a imagined commentator, authority, or different voice) to reveal a new facet of the setup and trigger another laugh. This is an intentional technique for variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect/respond to audience reaction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags can be reactive — commenting on or playing off the audience's immediate response (laughter, silence, heckle). Such responsiveness can create an additional comedic beat tied to the live moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optionality of tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags are optional; a joke can have many tags or none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tags where they add value (extra laughs or clarity). Don't add tags merely for quantity — unnecessary tags can dilute the joke's momentum or feel like padding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why tags matter / intended outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Build the funniness of the joke; maximize laughs from a single setup; mark a more sophisticated/experienced comedian; show the comedian 'thinking' about their own joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the goals to judge tags against: do they increase laugh volume/length, efficiently extract more laughs from a setup, demonstrate comic skill, or create the illusion of improvisational thought? Use these outcomes to decide whether a tag is successful.
